source: Kepler's Second Law: Equal Areas
A planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so it moves fastest when nearest the Sun.
Students think a planet moves at one steady speed around its orbit.
Kepler's first law gives the shape of an orbit. His second law tells how a planet moves along it, and the answer surprised him: not at a steady speed.

Imagine a line from the Sun to the planet. Kepler found that this line sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun the line is short, so to sweep a given area in a month the planet must cover a long stretch of its path: it moves fast. Far from the Sun the line is long, and a short stretch of path sweeps the same area: it moves slowly. Newton explained why. Gravity pulls straight toward the Sun, never sideways, so it never speeds up or slows down the planet's turning around the Sun (its angular momentum stays fixed). At perihelion and aphelion, where the motion is straight across the line to the Sun, this means $v_p\, r_p = v_a\, r_a$.
A planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so it moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion: $v_p\, r_p = v_a\, r_a$.
Equal areas in equal times: each gold wedge is swept in one-eighth of the orbit. The wedges near perihelion are short and wide; those near aphelion are long and thin.
Worked examples
Earth is $147.1$ million km from the Sun at perihelion (early January) and $152.1$ million km at aphelion (early July). How much faster does it move in January?
Earth's two speeds
About $1.034$ times as fast.
At the ends of the orbit: $\frac{v_p}{v_a} = \frac{r_a}{r_p}$.
Earth moves about $3.4\%$ faster in January, which is one reason northern winter is a few days shorter than northern summer.
A comet moves at $40$ km/s at perihelion, $0.5$ AU from the Sun. Its aphelion is $5$ AU out. How fast is it there?
A comet slows down
$v_a = v_p \cdot \frac{r_p}{r_a} = 40 \times \frac{0.5}{5}$.
$v_a = 4$ km/s: ten times farther, ten times slower.

It is natural to picture a planet cruising at one steady speed, but along an ellipse its speed changes all the time. Check with Earth: the March equinox to the September equinox (northern spring and summer, Earth farther out and slower) lasts about 186 days, while the other half of the year lasts about 179.
